text: Given a circular integer array nums, return the largest possible sum of a non-empty subarray. The end wraps around to the start, but each element can be used at most once.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a subarray is still contiguous, but now it can go past the last index and keep going from index zero. It can't be empty, and it can't use the same index twice. So the longest one is the whole array, once. And I only return the sum. Is that right?
Yes. Non-empty, at most once per element, and just the sum.

Okay. Then every answer is one of two shapes. Either it's a normal subarray in the middle, like the classic straight-line maximum subarray. Or it wraps: it takes a piece from the end and a piece from the start. And here's the trick. If a subarray wraps, then what it leaves out is one normal block in the middle. So the wrap sum is the total minus that middle block. I'll keep that in mind. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to three times ten to the fourth elements, and each value is between minus thirty thousand and plus thirty thousand.

Got it. So I want one pass. The biggest sum in size is thirty thousand times thirty thousand, nine hundred million — about forty-two percent of the int limit, so a plain int is enough. On the example, five, minus three, five, the normal best is the whole array, seven. But wrapping takes the last five and the first five and skips the minus three, for ten. And ten is exactly the total, seven, minus the skipped block, minus three. The other two examples give three, the three alone, and minus two, the single biggest number.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach tries every start index and walks up to n steps with the index wrapping modulo n. That's quadratic — correct, and I'd keep it as a brute force to test against, but too slow at thirty thousand elements. This problem reminds me of Kadane's algorithm — the extend-or-restart scan for maximum subarray on a straight line — and it covers the non-wrapping case directly. For the wrap case, I flip the question: instead of searching for the best wrap, I find the worst normal block, the minimum subarray, and cut it out. Total minus the minimum block is the best wrap, and the minimum comes from the same Kadane with min instead of max, in the same loop.

Here's the plan. One: track the total, plus cur-max and sub-max for the best block, cur-min and sub-min for the worst. Two: for each element, add it to the total, run extend-or-restart for both, and refresh the records. Three: if sub-max is below zero, return sub-max; otherwise return the larger of sub-max and total minus sub-min. One thing worth flagging — that guard. On minus three, minus two, minus three, the minimum block is the whole array, so total minus sub-min is zero — the empty subarray, which isn't allowed. The answer is minus two. And the guard must check sub-max, not the total: one, minus three, one has a negative total, yet the wrap gives two. A doubled array with a monotonic deque also works, but needs linear space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop: each element goes into the total, cur-max and cur-min each extend or restart, then sub-max and sub-min take any new record. After the loop, the guard returns sub-max if it's negative; otherwise I return the larger of total minus sub-min and sub-max. One thing worth flagging — the start values. Sub-max starts at the smallest int and sub-min at the largest, not zero — otherwise a lone minus one returns zero. Also, the last line still needs the max with sub-max: a single one would otherwise give zero, because the min block is the whole array again.

Let's dry-run the code with two, minus three, four, minus six, one, five — the wrap wins here, expected nine. The row that matters is index three, the minus six. For cur-min, extending gives minus five, but minus six alone is smaller, so it restarts — the worst block becomes just index three, and it never gets worse. At the end the total is three and sub-max is six, so no guard. Cut out the minus six: three minus minus six is nine, every index except three. Nine beats six, so nine. That matches. Corner cases: all negative returns minus two through the guard. One, minus two, three, minus two gives three, normal winning. Three, minus one, two, minus one ties at four. And all thirty thousands with one minus thirty thousand gives eight hundred ninety-nine million, nine hundred seventy thousand, which fits in an int.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, with both Kadanes in the same loop. Space is constant — five integers. There's no early exit, so it's always n steps, about forty microseconds at thirty thousand elements, and the biggest value I hold is nine hundred million, so no overflow. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the quadratic brute force. I ran about two hundred forty thousand cases with zero mismatches. That matters here: the wrong guard on the total passes all three official examples but fails on one, minus three, one, and a missing guard only breaks all-negative arrays. Bugs like that hide from hand-picked tests.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed the wrap case as the whole circle minus one middle block, so the best wrap is the total minus the minimum subarray, and you got both with one loop. You explained why the guard is needed: on an all-negative array the min block is the whole array, so total minus sub-min is zero — the empty subarray. And you showed the guard must check sub-max, not the total, with one, minus three, one. Good work.
